item.title: Scalable Unitary State-Encoding for Generic Large Data
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Amplitude-encoding state preparation simplifies multiplexer circuits to 1- and 2-qubit gates, reducing circuit depth by up to orders of magnitude at equivalent state fidelity compared to standard multiplexer methods.

Grade 0.426 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Vittorio Pagni, Peter K. Schuhmacher, Michael Felderer, Michael Epping, Kevin Lively

Figure

Ratio of CX-depth of the proposed Binary-Tree methods (BT-BE, BT-WHT, BT-Hybrid) to Qiskit's state-preparation circuit depth plotted against qubit count n across various target function families, demonstrating depth reductions of several orders of magnitude.

Asks

How can generic high-dimensional complex data or queryable functions be deterministically loaded into quantum states without exponential memory or circuit-depth overhead?

Before

Möttönen multiplexer-based state preparation decomposed generic states in Θ(N/n) depth via Shende recursive trees (as implemented in Qiskit), requiring dense storage of 2(2n−1) angles.

But

Boolean simplification involves an NP-hard optimization problem; Walsh-Hadamard method requires one clean ancilla qubit; memory reduction to O(2lχ2) relies on low Matrix Product State bond dimension χ.

Tools

Tensor Train / Matrix Product State representation · Tensor Cross Interpolation · Boolean logic Disjoint Sum of Products minimization · Walsh-Hadamard Transform · IQM superconducting quantum processor

Abstract

Efficient encoding of data into quantum states remains a fundamental bottleneck in many quantum computing protocols, which would otherwise offer advantages over their classical counterparts. Here, we introduce deterministic and scalable amplitude-encoding methods with low two-qubit gate costs and tunable trade-offs between circuit depth and encoding fidelity. Our approaches require no amplitude amplification or mid-circuit measurement and are capable of encoding arbitrary complex data or queryable functions by using tensor-networks to go beyond what can be held in classical memory. Our principle contributions are two complementary algorithms for simplifying fully controlled multiplexer circuits to one- and two-qubit gates. In the first, we formally map the elimination of redundant gate controls to a Boolean logic minimization problem, while in the second we utilize a single ancilla qubit to map the multi-controlled rotation gates to a sequence of one- and two-qubit operations via the Walsh-Hadamard spectrum of the gate angles. We benchmark these methods across a broad range of function classes, characterizing their total depth in an all-to-all connectivity graph against system size and target fidelity. Hybridizing our methods gives up to orders of magnitude improvement in circuit depth at equivalent state fidelity compared to the default state-preparation method in the Qiskit package. We furthermore demonstrate our method on IQM hardware with a square lattice connectivity, finding excellent fidelity, even with minimal noise mitigation. By significantly reducing gate depth for encoding, this work enables the experimental execution of applications on current and near-term hardware which would otherwise be reduced to noise before the first calculation step, shortening the time horizon to robust quantum utility.

item.title: Shared Lookups and Lazy Residues: Fewer Toffoli Gates for Factoring RSA-2048
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Factoring RSA-2048 uses 5.08×109 Toffoli gates at 1,461 peak logical qubits (15% reduction) and 2.55×109 Toffoli gates at 1,806 qubits (46% reduction).

Grade 0.419 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Monit Sharma, Hoong Chuin Lau

Figure

Fewest Toffoli gates per RSA-2048 factoring plotted against peak logical-qubit count. Blue points denote the new circuits and grey denotes the reference circuit evaluated across 534,240 parameter settings.

Asks

How many logical qubits and Toffoli gates are required to factor an RSA-2048 key when optimizing residue-arithmetic modular exponentiation?

Before

was 5.98×109 Toffolis at 1,461 qubits and 4.74×109 at 1,806 qubits (Gidney 2025)

But

Logical-circuit counts obtained via simulation; physical qubit and runtime projections depend on architecture-specific routing and compilation models without full layout validation.

Tools

multi-prime shared table lookups · residue checkpointing · lazy residue arithmetic · reference quantum circuit simulation benchmark

Abstract

Gidney's 2025 construction for factoring RSA-2048 with few logical qubits spends most of its Toffoli gates on discrete-log table lookups and residue uncomputation. We reduce both costs. Shared lookups return entries for several primes of a residue number system at once because they have the same address. Retained intermediate residues remove recomputation during cleanup and enable lazy arithmetic with a single final modular reduction. We prove output preservation and estimate resources with an open benchmark built on the reference simulator. Against the best reference setting within the same logical-qubit budget, using the published model for the reference and benchmark counts for our circuits, we obtain 15% fewer Toffolis at 1,461 qubits (5.08 ×10⁹ per factoring) and 46% fewer at 1,806 qubits (2.55 ×10⁹). A matched ablation finds 28.8% fewer Toffolis from three-prime sharing at fixed window and checkpoint settings. Architecture-specific timing determines how much becomes a runtime saving.

item.title: Twisted Compactification, Quotient Quantum Codes and Logical Gates
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Twisted compactification corresponds directly to quotient quantum codes; for 3D fermionic toric codes under a quarter-turn twist, it yields codes with linear distance starting at [[768,2,9]] hosting an explicit p+ip pump that acts logically as T up to Clifford factors.

Grade 0.419 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Po-Shen Hsin

Figure

Fundamental domain geometry of the quarter-turn compactified mapping torus TL2timesC4S1, whose quotient yields codes hosting the logical T gate via a p+ip pump.

Asks

How do topological twisted compactifications map systematically onto quotient quantum error-correcting codes, their logical operators, and their transversal gates?

But

Finite regular covers are required to describe the dressed Gauss laws as quotients. Invertible abelian gauge theories under twisting reach only quantum doubles D(G) with [G,G] central.

Tools

twisted compactification · deck group quotients · Tate cohomology · cup-product defects · spin-topological response formula

Abstract

Many quantum codes, including balanced-product, bivariate-bicycle and genon codes and the five-qubit code, are quotient codes: a larger code folded onto itself by identifying each check with its image under a deck transformation composed with a symmetry. We show that this is the lattice form of twisted compactification, in which a theory on X×F carries a symmetry background along F, and we use the correspondence in both directions. For monomial quotients of Pauli stabilizer codes, a transfer theorem gives the logical qudits, logical operators and distance bounds from those of the parent, with a Tate cohomology group counting the logical operators that are new. For higher-form and cup-product symmetries the twist is an entangling diagonal circuit; when a finite cover trivializes the background, the code is a dressed quotient, so abelian Pauli codes give non-abelian topological order such as D(D₄). The dressings have Clifford level at most one less than the degree of the twist, and for cubic twists the code dimension is a count of solutions of quadratic equations in cup products, which certifies that the code is not a Pauli stabilizer code when it is not a power of two; on tori and slabs the distance is linear in the size. Twists also create logical gates: three toric codes on S³ have no logical qubits, but on RP³ the same circuit is a logical CCZ. A quarter-turn twist of the 3D fermionic toric code gives codes of linear distance, from [[768,2,9]] up, whose p+ip pump is an explicit finite-time quasi-local evolution that preserves the code space exactly; using the spin-topological response formula of Barkeshli, Hsin and Kobayashi, we identify its logical action as T up to Clifford factors. Finally, twisting abelian gauge theories reach only the quantum doubles D(G) with [G,G] central.

item.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Parallel shuttling minimizes decoherence and leakage at short shuttling distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms it over long distances across 2-, 3-, and 4-spin encodings; multi-spin fidelity loss and leakage decompose analytically into sums of at most seven pairwise spin error parameters ϵjkP.

Grade 0.407 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Yu-Ning Zhang, Aleksandr S. Mokeev, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, David P. DiVincenzo, Viatcheslav V. Dobrovitski

Figure

Average fidelity loss 1−FXO of a 3-spin exchange-only qubit versus dimensionless shuttling length λ for sequential, parallel, and triangular protocols across channel separations δ=0.3,0.6,0.8. Parallel shuttling yields lower error at short range, whereas sequential shuttling wins at long range.

Asks

How do spatial and temporal correlations in magnetic noise affect dephasing and leakage during the shuttling of multi-spin logical qubits across different trajectories?

But

Pure dephasing via rotating-frame secular Hamiltonian (neglecting x,y noise and spin relaxation). Neglects inter-spin exchange interaction during shuttling. Assumes stationary, isotropic Gaussian noise field.

Tools

Gaussian random field model of spatio-temporal 1/f noise · mixed-unitary dephasing quantum channel · pairwise dephasing factor expansion · Pauli transfer matrix analysis

Abstract

Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated 1/f noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

item.title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
item.description:
Worth a look new result — 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes with 53≤n≤254 and 5≤d≤13 exceed the lower distance bounds in Grassl's tables, raising 1,873 table entries by standard propagation rules. Expurgated random codes yield roughly 8 more logical qubits than typical random codes.

Grade 0.396 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation” · Marin Girard

Figure

Plots generator count n−k versus code length n across distances d=5 to 13. Shows the 192 new codes beating the existing table entries in regions where the table codes matched the Gilbert-Varshamov bound.

Asks

Can random stabilizer codes improved by expurgation beat the best known lower bounds recorded in Grassl's qubit code tables?

Before

Grassl's tables (as of 4 November 2026); 161 codes beat the table's distance by 1 and 31 beat it by 2, yielding gains of up to 9 logical qubits at fixed (n,d) where the table was near the Gilbert-Varshamov bound.

But

Certifying distance requires exhaustively checking up to 4.2×1013 Pauli operators, scaling in time and memory as nd/2 (requiring supercomputer clusters for n≈250,d≈13); codes have dense check matrices.

Tools

Random Clifford encoders · Stabilizer expurgation · Meet-in-the-middle exhaustive syndrome enumeration · Aurora supercomputer

Abstract

I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes [[n,k,d]] with 53≤n≤254 and 5≤d≤13 whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same (n,k): 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to 4×10¹³ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight d. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at d≥9 and ngtrsim170, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs (n,d). The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.

item.title: Beyond the n/2 Threshold: Quantum Query Complexity for Computing Hamming Weight and Symmetric Functions
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Recovering exact Hamming weight and computing any symmetric Boolean function takes at most n/2+O(n1/3) quantum queries with bounded error; explicit symmetric functions require n/2+Ω(n1/3) queries.

Grade 0.392 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers in 8 hours using 20 million noisy qubits” · Yuan Deng, Zihan Hao, Honghao Lin, Qipeng Liu, Vahab Mirrokni, Jianan Shao, David P. Woodruff

Figure

Schematic of the symmetric functions F2m,0 and F2m,R across input Hamming weights, highlighting the central zero-valued plateaus of width 2 and 2R+2 adjacent to alternating tail regions.

Asks

Is any additive overhead beyond n/2 unavoidable for quantum query algorithms computing a single Boolean output, and what is its optimal worst-case order?

Before

was n/2+O(n) queries for all Boolean functions via oracle interrogation (van Dam 1998)

But

Worst-case query complexity; bounded constant error; lower bound proven for symmetric Boolean functions.

Tools

quantum counting · Grover search · coherent quantum walk on matchings · one-query parity sampling

Abstract

The oracle-interrogation algorithm [van Dam, FOCS '98] computes every n-bit Boolean function with bounded error using n/2+O(√n) quantum queries. In contrast, parity can be computed exactly using lceiln/2rceil queries, but whether an additive overhead beyond n/2 is necessary for a single Boolean output has remained open. In this work, we construct an explicit family of symmetric Boolean functions requiring n/2+Ω(n^(1/3)) quantum queries at a fixed positive constant error. We also give an algorithm that recovers the exact Hamming weight using n/2+O(n^(1/3)) quantum queries with bounded error, and therefore computes every symmetric Boolean function within the same query bound. Together, these results determine the optimal additive order for Hamming weight recovery and for the worst case over symmetric Boolean functions at sufficiently small constant error.

item.arxave:abstract: The oracle-interrogation algorithm [van Dam, FOCS '98] computes every n-bit Boolean function with bounded error using n/2+O(√n) quantum queries. In contrast, parity can be computed exactly using lceiln/2rceil queries, but whether an additive overhead beyond n/2 is necessary for a single Boolean output has remained open. In this work, we construct an explicit family of symmetric Boolean functions requiring n/2+Ω(n^(1/3)) quantum queries at a fixed positive constant error. We also give an algorithm that recovers the exact Hamming weight using n/2+O(n^(1/3)) quantum queries with bounded error, and therefore computes every symmetric Boolean function within the same query bound. Together, these results determine the optimal additive order for Hamming weight recovery and for the worst case over symmetric Boolean functions at sufficiently small constant error.
